We are told that the amount paid by the government to the Grand Trunk Pacific for the surveys they made before the government took over the eastern division was $352,191.75, and that the amount which the surveys have cost which were executed under the authority of the government-the government surveys-is $3,381,072.41; a pretty round sum, Mr. Speaker, as you will notice. It is not out of place to add to it the $352,191.75 paid to the railway company, and to call attention to the fact that although we are paying for the surveys of this line, almost $4,000,000, the government newspapers and many of the supporters of the government are now taking the attitude that this survey was not expected to be in any sense conclusive, to be that it was merely a preliminary canter, and that the estimates founded on these surveys were not to be expected to be definite to any degree, were mere guess work, that the quantities of solid rock, loose rock and common excavation entering into the construction of the work were merely hazard and guess.
The total expenditure for supervising and overseeing the construction of the work, the staff of engineers placed in charge by the government amounts to $3,699,796.01.
The cost of the commissioners' office will be interesting to the House, and to the public. The singularly efficient way in which these gentlemen are discharging their duties in the public interest, the peculiar qualifications which they possess for that position, the special knowledge they have of railway building, render it interesting to know how much we pay for the carrying on of this office. We are told that we have paid, down to March 31, for the office of the commissioners, and their rentals, staffs, &c., $1,307,250. We are told that we are paying for our share of rentals at Winnipeg, $85,312.
Then as to the cost of the Quebec bridge which collapsed, I need not give the details which are well known. In round figures it is $7,000,000. The cost of investigating the collapse of the bridge was $31,765.44. The cost of plans and investigations preliminary to letting the new contract amounts to $149,087.75.
Coming to the position of the Transcontinental railway at present we are faced by the broad fact which must be admitted by every o.ne on either side of the controversy that there has been an enormous and startling discrepancy between the estimated expenditure upon this road, and the alleged actual expenditure. The sums that are being allowed, and that are being paid out for the work from Moncton to Winnipeg

may possibly be honest, and fair or they may not be, but the whole proposition is inevitably inconsistent with the belief that we had fair, honest, reliable information at the time that this scheme was launched, and again at the time the surveys were made, and that these returns are also correct and honest. If the information that we have obtained as to the facilities for railway construction was honestly announced by the government in 1903 and 1904, if the surveys arid explorations which have cost this country about $4,000,000 were of any value at all, then there is cogent evidence that the 'amount that is being paid for this railway 'scheme is far too great. I propose to-day to call the attention of the House to the basis upon which the country was committed to this scheme, and to ask that an inquiry shall be made now into' whether or not the large expenditure that is being made for the construction of this road is justifiable, and in the public interest. To do that I shall have to refer to statements that have been made by prominent members of the government. I wish to repeat a remark that brought forth cries of ' No, oh, oh,' on a recent occasion, that the government distinctly pledged the people that the total outlay of Canada, the total amount which Canada would be out of pocket, would not exceed $13,000,000. I am not going to confuse the issue between the cost of constructing the work, and the amount Canada was to pay, and be out of pocket, but I repeat what is constantly denied upon the public platform -and I propose to prove it-that the government clearly and distinctly pledged itself to the people that all the money that this scheme would cost Canada for the Transcontinental Tailway, from ocean to ocean, would be $13,000,000, and not one cent more.
The hon. member is not serious when he says that.

I am as serious as my hon. friend, and I think I am a good deal more wise, because if the hon. gentleman will study this question instead of talking at random he must find that the evidence is so cogent and irresistible that he will have to admit it. However, let us go by the records. I desire also to call attention to 'the statements' in reference to the character of the country through which the road will be built, and shall read from statements of only two or three of the ministers. The Prime Minister said :
In that consideration alone there would have been cause sufficient for us to go on with this work without any previous explorations, but I have to say this more, that we have a wealth of information on this subject. We have more information upon this scheme than
ever was possessed by former governments when they decided the Intercolonial railway or the Canadian Pacific railway.
He goes on to point out that east of the Quebec boundary the land is 'well adapted for cultivation and farming and almost an unbroken stretch of good farming land. Then he deals with the land through which Mr. McArthur is building his 240 miles of railway and says:
The country east of Lake Abitibi has also been explored, and explored several times. .
. . The Quebec government had it explored in the last few years by an engineer of eminence, Mr. O'Sullivan, and his opinion has been summarized by another engineer, Mr. Doucet, with the following language: ' From Roberval (which is a station on the Quebec and Lake St. John railway) to the western limit of the province of Quebec, a distance of some 375 miles, the line runs through a good farming country, the soil being chiefly clay.'
I need not continue the quotation, because what follows is simply an amplification of this sentence. He says:
This is a sample of the whole.
Then the right lion, gentleman quoting from Mr. Farrell:
It is established that the region between Winnipeg and Quebec is a fertile clay belt rich in good land, rich in timber, rich in powers, rich in all those resources which go to make a fine agricultural and industrial country. Such being the facts

And it is very important to inquire if they are facts, because if they are facts they are utterly inconsistent with the proposition that we have practically 1,800 miles of solid rock road bed for the eastern division of the Transcontinental railway-
Such being the facts, what is the conclusion to be drawn from them? The conclusion seems to be obvious and imperative, that is, that we must at once provide for a railway to tap these rich and fertile territories.
Farther on, the Prime Minister deals with the question of cost, and I would like to challenge my hon. friend who interrujpt-ed me a moment ago to get up in the House and refute the statement that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance made it as clear and as emphatic as a proposition could possibly be made, that the total money cost to Canada would1 be between $12,000,000 and $13,000,000, and not a cent more. This is what the Prime Minister said:
Assuming the road across the mountains is 600 miles long, the cost of construction will be $18,000,000, and the total interest for three years will be $3,780,000. This is the whole of the liability which is incurred by the government for the construction of the railway from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean.

I understand that the Tight hon. gentleman meant independent of the guarantee on which he had stated that we would not ultimately lose one cent. Then, coming to the eastern division, he said:
The same abatement of rent is provided also as in the case of interest on the western section. During seven years the company will he exempt from the payment of rent, so that here again the whole of the liability which is incurred by the government for the building of that section from Moncton to Winnipeg is simply seven years' interest. The sum total of the money to be paid by the government for the construction of that line from Moncton to the Pacific ocean will be in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, and not a cent more.
Is that reasonably definite for my hon. friend? He said further:
Now, Sir, what is $13,000,000 in the year 1903? It is about the surplus of our revenue over the expenditure. The surplus for this year will pay for the construction of this road.
What the right hon. gentleman said then was correct- $13,000,000 in 1903 was $13,000,000; but when we come in 1910. it has grown as the Tock has grown, and it has grown into what would appear to be a fabulous sum were it not that I can prove and establish it by the records handed out by the government from time to time. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very important question at this juncture, and it is fair to see upon what pledges the government *committed us to this scheme, for the purpose of insisting on the government giving evidence of their good faith in What they then stated ; and, having regard to the subsequent developments which are now on record, we believe that it is full time that we should have some inquiry to see how these enormous discrepancies were brought about. As to the general character of the country, the right hon. gentleman said :
The information we have at this moment is to the effect that for three-fourths of the distance between Quebec and Winnipeg the line will run over a level plateau over which the construction of a railway will be almost as feasible as over the prairies. But even as to the general character of the country we have to-day abundant information that it is possessed of a character in regard to soil and climate which will be a painful disappointment to those gentlemen who have taken a morbid pleasure in maligning it.
It ought to be a painful disappointment to the government to find that for some cause, honest or dishonest, I know not which, the character which has been stamped on that country by the returns as to the expenditure is the very opposite of that Mr. LENNOX.

Once upon a time I made the statement on the floor of this House that we had in regard to this tract of country mountains of information. That statement was received with a great deal of sneering incredulity.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the returns which are being sent in from time to time in regard to the construction of this road are accurate,, as the government supporters , have been contending, were we not rather wise in sneering with a good deal of incredulity at the statements of my right hon. friend and his government at that time? This is the character of the country that new railway will cross.
It will be recollected that the opposition did not oppose this scheme in toto; they were as anxious as were the government to construct a railway for the purpose of carrying the grain of the west to the markets of the world. But the opposition thought it was wise to have some necessary explanations, some preliminary investigations, some data more reliable than the flowery language of gentlemen who happened to see one or two spots of the country. But my right hon. friend, anticipating how reasonable would be that demand, before we ever made the demand, before he sat down after making his delivery upon the occasion of introducing this project, used this language. It is very striking, very picturesque," but it is not so distinctly characterized by good judgment or common sense:

To those who urge upon us the policy of to-morrow and to-morrow, those who tell us wait, wait, wait, to those who advise us to pause, to consider, to reflect, to calculate, our answer is, no, this is not the time for deliberation, this is the time for action.
And we have evidence now of how wise was the course taken by the government.

This is without interest. Now, taking the actual facts as they have turned out, and still counting without interest, what do we find? Taking the figures furnished us by the government, and which I will refer to later on, we find that the road has actually cost $153,920,100, or more than $85,000 a mile. That is the difference- on that basis. Now, I might refer just for a moment to the western division, and I do so because it emphasizes very clearly how egregiously the government has erred in its calculations. And there is a very significant parallel. It was represented that what, as a matter of fact, we were to pay as a subsidy for the western division of the railway through that wonderfully rich country-and what must be a paying proposition-was $3,024,000. As a matter of fact we are paying for that portion of the road $13,690,000, or practically the same money as the Finance Minister said we

should have to pay both for the eastern division-with highest grade of construction-and as subsidy for the western division as well. Before I deal more fully with that, let me quote a word or two from the Prime Minister again. Those who were in the House at that time will remember in what a jaunty iway the Prime Minister introduced the amendments which were agreed upon between the session of 1903, and the session of 1904. He said it was a little thing, in fact that the opposition would be disappointed because it was so little. Here is what he said, speaking of the amendments proposed:
The propositions which they made to us and the concessions which were made bv us are now before the House. They are not numerous, and I venture to say that our honourable friends opposite, when they saw the narrow extent of the concessions which we had agreed to, were surprised at the moderation of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the comparatively unimportant modifications which we were called upon to make. Not only were they surprised at the moderation of the concessions which we made, but I believe they were vexed, because it deprived them of a good deal of the thunder which they were prepared to fulminate here.
Mr. Speaker, you represent that rich and beautiful county of Bonaventure. I represent a great riding, that of South Sim-coe. When we reflect that, by a wave of his hand, the Prime Minister was giving away practically the value of a county, I am not quite disposed to join with him in speaking of the great moderation of these proposals. When the Prime Minister tells us that we are practically giving no important concession, I call attention to the fact that we were increasing our liability then from $25,000,000 to $55,000,000, or a difference of $30,000,000; and we are increasing our cash contributions- from $5,285,700 to $13,690,000, or a difference of $8,404,300. Now, that brings us to this proposition, that in so far as the western division is concerned we are paying for the construction of that branch of the railway in cash as much as the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister said we would pay as our contribution to the entire scheme. Now, as to our actual cash contribution to this railway scheme, taking it as a whole, it figures out in this way: We are paying interest seven years on bonds for the mountain section, $13,690,000; we are paying interest on cost of construction of the eastern division for seven years, $42,690,560; interest on unreported expenditure, say, $1,000,000; investigations, legal expenses, etc., $500,000, making a total of $57,880,560. Then between the actuarial figures as given by the Finance Minister and the actual round sum at which the amount appears to stand, the difference after all is only between 10 and 11 per cent. Making a computation on the same basis and taking off upwards of $5,000,000, we have $52,000,000 left as the actual cash outlay that Canada will pay on undisputed items, or four times the amount at which the Finance Minister and the Prime Minister put it. If you add our share of the Quebec bridge, the four-ninths the Finance Minister said that we would be called upon to charge against this scheme, and if we add the difference in interest, one-quarter per cent, for 43 years during which we borrow money at probably 34 per cent and only receive back 3 per cent as rental, we wiil have $76,000,000, or six times the amount that the government said we would have to pay.
Now we have this fact to consider. After the government had made these declarations, then we had the surveys, costing about $4,000,000, and the engineers' reports to the government, and on these the contracts' were let. At that time, for all the items that were embraced in those contracts, the engineers estimated the total cost would be in round figures $65,000,000. Taking those same figures, the actual working out shows that instead of costing $65,000,000, the road cost us $105,000,000, a very good reason for believing that there may be a good deal in the proposition which the government is so sedulously advancing now that the expensive surveys which we had there after all were only guess work, that the government was working in the dark. Now, in reference to that, assuming that the surveys were really guess work, I would like to show you upon high authority how fatal

a matter that kind of thing ia. There was a royal commission appointed after a portion of the Canadian Pacific railway was built, that is, the portions built by the government, and Judge Clark and some other prominent gentlemen, Mr. Keefer and Mr. Miall, composed the commission. It was argued in the course of that investigation that it was not necessary to have accurate surveys before the work was let to contractors. It was pointed out, that there were investigations much more thorough than these surveys are now alleged to have been made by this government. They said:
During the progress of the evidence it has transpired that in the case of the first four contracts for roadbed construction between Thunder bay and Red river, tenders were invited and contracts let before sufficient examination had been made of the projected line to enable the engineering department to state, in most cases, even approximately, what work would require to be performed.
The bills of works offered to tenderers were invariably calculated from nothing more reliable than profile plans. In every case the contract was let before the quantities had been made up from cross-sections.
Now, the government has the hardihood in certain quarters to put forward the statement that in some cases there was no profile plan at all, and what is more essential, that in some cases there was no location before this work was let to contract. They are either on one horn of the dilemma or the other; they neglected their duty to the people or else the statement put forward is a subterfuge to deceive the people. It was contended, however, in the Canadian Pacific railway case, that it made no difference. The commission said:
The evidence leads us to a different conclusion. If the quantities upon which the tender is based should turn out to be approximately correct, and the various tenders consistent as to prices, the relative position of the tenders, when subsequently based on executed quantities, might not undergo much change, but should the prices affixed to the tenders be incongruous and the relative proportions of earth excavation, rock, masonry, &c., bo materially altered during the process of construction, then those tenders which seemed to be the lowest might turn out to be considerably higher than others.
That is just what happened in this case.

I submit and charge that the attitude of the government, and commission in regard to _ persons making complaints of wrong doing in the carrying out of the work- notably in the cases of Major Hodgins and Mr. Lumsden-is calculated to deter engineers, and others in charge, from effeci-ently, honestly and fearlessly discharging their duties, tends to encourage dishonesty, and the allowance and payment of unjust claims, is distinctly opposed to the public interest, and is deserving of the severest censure.
The enormous differences shown to exist between ithe estimated, and pledged expenditure, and the alleged or actual cost are far too great to be accounted for upon any basis of reasonable error-they necessarily involve, upon the part of those having the initiation, management, and carrying out of the work, ot of many of them: incompetency, or dishonesty, or both; and are of such grave public concern as ito demand an immediate and thorough investigation into the circumstances under which this undertaking was launched, and the causes -which have brought about this unwarranted expenditure of public money.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, in concluding with a motion, I will ask that the House shall appoint a royal commission to investigate the whole matter; and let me say, although I have not incorporated it in my motion, because I think it will better come in this form, that I demand on behalf of the public that it shall be a fair appointment, and that the people shall have a fair chance. And let the criticism be what it will, I know with what vile criticism we were met when we demanded what were the people's rights in the Lumsden investigation. I have no fear of criticism either at the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite or at any other hands. I claim that no investigation will be satisfactory to the members of the opposition-that is not important, but no investigation will be satisfactory to the public-which does not recognize three or four essential conditions to which I will refer. One of them is that the leader of the opposition shall be conceded the right of nominating at least a minority of the commission. It is beyond question that it will be the government that will be on trial, and it is manifestly in the public interest and manifestly just that the proposition that I submit in that regard should be conceded. Further, no commission will be satisfactory or will command the public confidence unless the opposition are afforded reasonable means of bringing forward the evidence necessary to thoroughly sift the question as to whether too much money is being paid or not. To that end it will be right and just, and we will demand-or at least, speaking for

myself, I demand, and I'believe the people will demand-that the leader of the opposition shall have the right, not only to engage reasonable professional assistance in the nature of engineering experts, but also to nominate at least one or two of the counsel who shall be engaged in the prosecution of the inquiry. I have outlined as briefly as I could, and I am sorry I could not make it more brief, the situation as it presents itself to-day. I am not putting it as a question whether the government is guilty or not guilty, but I am saying that the government is on trial today in the minds of the people of the Dominion of Canada, and I am asking that the people shall put upon trial those who have misrepresented, intentionally or otherwise, the true situation, or who are maintaining in the management of the construction of this road those who must be squandering the people's money and defrauding the people of their just rights.
I, therefore, move, seconded by Mr. Blain:
That all the words after the word 'that' in the proposed motion be left out and the following substituted therefor:
1.	In the debate upon the proposed construction of the National Transcontinental Railway in 1903 and 1904, the Prime Minister and other members of the government declared that they had gone thoroughly into the whole question, and were in possession of abundant, expert and general information as to the character of the country through which the road would be built; that 'for three-fourths of the distance between Quebec and Winnipeg the line would be run over a level plateau over which the construction of a railway was almost as feasible as over the prairies;' that the government were then competent, to correctly judge as to the extent of the undertaking and its cost; that delay for investigation was unnecessary and inexpedient, and that they had definitely ascertained that the total cost, to Canada, would not exceed $13,000,000.
2.	That the Minister of Finance in the session of 1903 expressly professing to speak upon reliable information from competent expert authorities, declared to parliament that the actual cost of the eastern division would amount to no more than $51,300,000, or including interest during construction to the sum of $54,609,676; and moreover that with a grade of four tenths of one per cent, about 21 feet to the mile, and construction accord ing to the highest known standards the cost without interest would not exceed $61,640,000, or an average of $34,170 per mile.
3.	According to official returns since laid upon the table of the House this eastern division, without counting anything for interest, and with many items of construction as yet not included, will cost not less than $154,000,000, or an average of more than $85,000 per mile.
4.	According to these official returns and statements of ministers, the total cost of the eastern division will actually amount to not
less than the sum of $218,467,314, made up as
follows:-
Payments under 21 contracts.. .. $104,530,905 Four-ninths share of the cost of
the Quebec bridges	 7,594,091
Terminals at Quebec	 2,000,000
Share of terminals at	Winnipeg. 1,156,252
Share of shops at Moncton	 750,000
Share of terminal yards at Moncton	 97,000
Numerous items (not covered by contracts) as per statement recently furnished by the government	 37,797,852
Total exclusive of interest.. $153,926,100
Interest on outlay during one-half period of construction, that is average of four years' simple interest at 31 per cent	 21,549,654
Cost at time road to be handed
over to company	$175,475,754
Add interest at 3| per cent for seven years after road handed over, during which country is to bear the charge	 42,991,560
Total at end 7 years' period. $218,467,314
Making an average expenditure of more than $120,000 a mile, and representing a fixed annual charge of $6,554,020.
5.	To this cost of construction, and to interest account, must be added very large sums for entry into Winnipeg, for locomotive accommodation there; also for additional terminal requirements at Moncton and at other points; and for further probable interest charges.
6.	According to the estimates upon which the contracts were awarded for the eastern division, rock excavation was to cost $23,322,976, whereas according to the official returns now brought down, the cost of such rock excavation alone upon that division will be not less than $52,000,000, a sum exceeding the Finance Minister's estimated full cost of the complete construction of this part of the road; and in many cases the contractor is being paid for rock work alone more than he was supposed to be entitled to be paid for fully completing all work upon his section.
7.	Taking interest account alone computed on the actuarial basis adopted by the Minister of Finance, and granting that the company may take over the road and pay the stipulated rental, and leaving out of account our annual loss on the difference between the rate of rent received and the rate of interest paid out for forty-three years, Canada will be out of pocket in actual cash an amount more than four times as great as the amount stated to parliament as the cost to Canada for the purpose of inducing parliament to approve and pass the Transcontinental legislation.
8.	That having regard to the astounding and unexplained increase in the cost of the said railway it is absolutely essential in the public interest that there should be a broad and thorough investigation into all matters

connected with the building of the eastern division of the Transcontinental railway.
9.	Therefore this House is of the opinion that a royal commission consisting of not less than three competent persons should be appointed to make inquiry into and concerning all the facts and circumstances connected with the inception of the Transcontinental railway project and undertaking, the conduct and efficiency of the various persons acting for the government or the country, the mode in which the work has been carried on both from an engineering and financial point of view, the manner in which the commissioners and the various officials and employees have discharged their duties, the manner in which contracts have been entered into and executed, accounts verified and payments made from time to time, and generally an inquiry into all facts and circumstances relating to or affecting the public interest in regard to the undertaking, with all powers usual in such cases including those provided for in an Act respecting inquiries into public matters.
10.	That this House is also of opinion that the government should take immediate and effective action to investigate the danger of diversion of Canadian traffic to foreign parts and to prevent any such diversion.
I may say that the concluding part of the resolution is based upon the form of order made in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway investigation already referred to.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) on his industry, which is only exceeded by his imagination. If there were a fund earmarked for the destruction and not the construction of this great international undertaking, my hon. friend's indemnity might well be charged to that fund, because he has spent his whole time this session and most of it last session in digging and delving to see if he could not find something somewhere which he could add to the accumulation of injurious things that have been said about this great national work, said by companies and their agents on the other side of the line who are interested in not having this constructed, said by others who are interested in not having this road constructed, and reiterated by hon. gentlemen in this House, not with the object, perhaps, of injuring the undertaking, but with an object which can only be attained through the injury of this great undertaking. I imagined that once the Canadian people had approved of this project everything possible that could be said against it had been said, that the representatives of the people, no matter what their politics might be, would take some pride in this undertaking which is to assist in making Canada one of the greatest dominions in the British empire. But, no, Sir, every possible straw is grasped

in order to make it appear as if this road should never have been constructed at all in its entirety, and these attempts having failed and the people having given a mandate to build the road, the object of the attack has since been against the method of constructing the road and against its cost. Now, I just want to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) that the only thing that can be attained, if his words have any influence at all, and I do not think they will have, the only object that can be attained by such a speech is to make it difficult for the great company associated with this undertaking to carry on its finances in the old land. That is the only thing that could be attained. All that he has said to-day has been said before by able men on the platforms throughout the country, and has been written by hired men who filled columns of the newspapers in the United States, copies of which papers were spread broadcast throughout Canada. But in face of all that, the people of Canada said again, knowing all this, we want Sir Wilfrid to finish his work and to go on and complete-the Transcontinental. I am happy to say to the members of this House and to the Dominion of Canada, that the results that followed the attacks on this undertaking in the year 1908, still remain. that is. the attacks have no effect at all. because after a discussion only yesterday with the president of the Grand Trunk railway, who has just returned from the old land, I am happy to say that the financial standing of that organization is good, and that the work will pe carried out speedily. I am surprised at my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox), who is usually mild-mannered, using the long line of expletives which he has introduced into the concluding part of his speech. I noticed that he read that part where the large adjectives were, which leads me to believe that in his own mild wav he could never have used them in making an address if he had not carefully written them out previously. In all my' experience of public life, which extends over a few years, I have never listened to a more unfair presentation of a case than that of my hon. friend this afternoon. I say that advisedly. The insinuations made about men just as honourable as any member of this House, just as respectable, just as capable, were not called for, and should not have been made by any man unless he meant to make a distinct charge and face the issue squarely, The figures quoted about the .cost of the line, concerning which there was a difference of opinion. I say, are misleading to the House and to the country, and I think I can prove to the House that the inference drawn from those figures by my hon. friend were not warranted by the figures themselves

The first part of my hon. friend's remarks were entirely ancient history. He dealt with the assertions of the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and others as to what this road would cost. That has been threshed out time and time again. This resolution which the hon. member has presented, may be divided into two parts- possibly three. The first we might call the substructure-the recital found in sections 1 and 2. The rest we may call the superstructure, except the last section, which may be not unfitly termed the tower, because I think it was put on at the last as an afterthought. I am inclined to think that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition added the last clause as a sort of antidote to his anti-conduct on a Canadian-made navy; I take it that it is intended rather for consumption in Halifax and the maritime provinces as an offset to the hon. gentleman's position on the naval question.
Now, let me deal with these sections as I have outlined them. In the first place, there is the substructure, this long recital found in sections 1 and 2. This House is asked to vote seriously upon the statement that the Prime Minister tried to induce the House and the country to believe that this road would cost but $13,000,000. No matter what play there may be with words, that ha3 been laughed out of this House, it has been laughed off the platforms of Canada, it has been laughed out of public discussion by the people. Did that statement deceive any hon. member of this House? My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart) stated that the road would cost $125,000,000, and, speaking in all fairness, notwithstanding the remarks of my hon. friend from South Simcoe, I say that if I wanted an accurate statement as to the co3t of railway construction or any other accurate information in that line, I would prefer to take the statement of the hon. member for South Lanark, probably, to that of any other man in this House. My hon. friend from East Grey made the same statement-that the cost would be $125,000,000. These hon. members were not deceived. I think that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) estimated that the addition to the debt of Canada as the result of this construction would be in the region of $100,000,000, but I think he said it would be impossible to estimate it within $10,000,000. So, these leading members on the other side were not deceived by anything said on this side into believing that the cost of the road would be only $13,000,000. But, I want to show by the words of the hon. member for South Simcoe himself that he acknowledged in this House that he knew better, that he knew that what the Prime Minister intended to convey was not the entire cost of the road, but something entirely different. I will read his expla-262
nation. On this point of an estimate of $13,000,000 he said:
We the members of this House understood that the Prime Minister did not mean that the total expenditure in the construction of the road would be $13,000,000. He intended to convey the proposition that the money that would be paid and not received back would be $13,000,000.
Now, my hon. friend from South Simcoe himself acknowledged what everybody else acknowledges. And while I am not surprised that hon. gentlemen opposite should occasionally refer to it, I am surprised at them seriously placing that statement as a clause in a resolution on which they ask the members of this House to vote. There i3 not a member of this House who believes that the attempt was made -to convince them that the entire cost of the road would be $13,000,000-not one. And I give the public credit for knowing as much as I do about these matters, or as much as any member of this House.
Now, take section 2 of the resolution. My hon. friend gives here the statement of the Minister of Finance and proceeds to make that the foundation for some other clauses. The Finance Minister gave an estimate to the House based on the opinion of an engineer; and my hon. friend from South Simcoe will not gainsay the character, the reputation, the honour, the ability of that engineer, Mr. Schreiber. The Minister of Finance like every other hon. member, other hon. members who had had practical experience, like my hon. friend for South Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart), made their statements on our estimate of the chief engineer. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) might as well have iplaced in the resolution a clause referring to the statements of other members who made estimates. And when he assumes to attack the Finance Minister because he gave an estimate given to him by a man as prominent as Mr. Schreiber, and asks this House, and asks an intelligent public, to believe that he is seriously making that a reason for this resolution, he is going a long way indeed.
Now, I come to section No. 3, and I am getting along to what might be called the superstructure. The hon. member goes into a series of figures, and makes a statement from the official returns. I am not going to quarrel with that part of the statement or dissect his figures, but I think a very short consideration of the matter will show that I have been so generous in bringing down figures for my hon. friend's consideration that he has got lost in the mazes of the calculation.
That might easily be.

The hon. member figures out that this road will cost $85,000 per



mile. Now, let us stop right there for a moment. I do not concede that this estimate is correct. But, if it were correct, what about it? Has the hon. member the right to make this the basis of abuse of every person who has had to do with the road? I say, no. Let him look up the cost of building railways at a time when material was not nearly so expensive or labour nearly so high as at present. Let me give a few samples of what roads have cost in years gone by. In New South Wales, the roads have cost $64,000 a mile; in Germany, $107,000 a mile; in France, $126,000 a mile; in Italy, $109,000 a mile; in Russia, $83,000 a mile; in Austria-Hungary $87,000 a mile; in Great Britain and Ireland, $272,000 a mile. And in the United States, with all their poor railways, with all their small branch lines, where some have grades of one to twu and a half per cent, where some have 67-pound rails, where they have no compensation on the curves or grades-the cheapest kind of road [DOT]-and even there the roads have cost on the average $58,000 a mile. And take the Dominion of Canada. My hon. friend will know that we have in this Dominion some very poor roads, improving it is true, but some of them even yet mere colonization roads with 50-pound rails, very little ballasting, and the cheapest of construction. If my hon. friend will look into it, he will find that the average cost of these roads in Canada, including cheaper colonization roads is $56,000 a mile. Take the Intercolonial-and my hon. friend will not complain if I use this as a comparison for his friends had something to do with the construction of that line as well as ours-the Intercolonial has cost for construction $63,000 a mile. So, I say, if I stopped at that point, if I took the figuies given by the hon. member, together with the quality and standard of this road from Moncton to Winnipeg, and assume that we have a road of that kind at a cost of $85,000 a mile, I say it will stand comparison with the construction of any railway system in the Dominion of Canada or on the continent of America.
May I ask a question?
Yes.
Did the government know of the cost of these other roads at the time when they gave these assurances to parliament? Had they taken the trouble to investigate the question to that extent?

The hon. member (Mr. R. L. Borden) is asking me a question that he knows I am not in a position to answer. If I could tell what was in his mind when Mr. GRAHAM.
he made his estimate, I might have some sort of mental telepathic knowledge that would tell me what the government were thinking about before I became a member of it.
Does the minister (Mr. Graham) think that they ought to have investigated the question to that extent?

Possibly they did. Whether they did or not, I am stating the facts. If they had not investigated, the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) should have given them this information, when he discussed the matter, because, no doubt, the opposition knew all about it. Now, we come to No. 4, and I want to say candidly that I cannot quite see how the hon. member reached the figure of $104,530,905 in his resolution.

I will tell the hon. minister, if I can be of any use to him. I got it by taking thirteen contracts with the amount that has been expended, and the amount reported as necessary to complete them. I add these together. Then, I assumed, as I stated, that on the other contracts on which work will be done will amount to about the same.

I do not find fault with my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox), because I can understand his difficulty in arriving at the results. I do not intend to go into all these figures, but I may say that there is a mistake of $16,000,000 in this one item. Now, I will take up those figures without going into details. On that item there is a mistake of something like $16,000,000. I think he took $67,890,697 up to December 31, as including only the twenty-one contracts, while as a matter of fact it included $20,358,679 that had been spent on items not in the contracts.

No, I took what the returns show as being expended, and what is yet to be expended, I added these two together, I took 13 contracts, because there are only 13 contracts on whieh there appears to have been considerable work done. I add the two sets of figures together, and I find they amount to some $60,000,000, while they were to have cost about *17.000. That means that they are actu-allv costing at the rate of 62-8 per cent more than they were to have cost. I assume those on which very little work has been done will work out as I said on about the same basis. The minister, with the greater information, may be able to show that they do not work out on exactly the same basis. It may be that the warnings these parties have got have already had some effect.

If my hon. friend is through, perhaps he will now allow me to proceed. Now, I will try and point out wherein my hon. friend's figures may be inaccurate. In making his estimate he was pretty positive, because he figured interest on these items. By his method of calculation, which I have now found out, a man could figure himself into affluence or penury in fifteen minutes if he had a good strong pencil, by adding a lot more to his revenue and capital expenditure on which interest must be charged. Now the amount actually paid up to December 21, 1909, on these 21 contracts is $48,578,614.19. The contract reserve-my hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) will understand what that means-the contract reserve is $3,247,295. The estimate made by the chief engineer to complete is $35,949,958; total $87,775,867.19. But there was an amount omitted in the December estimates of $929,721.57. This makes a total $88,705,588.76 as against the $104,530,905; consequently there is an error in the first item of $15,825,317, if the chief engineer's estimate be accurate.

In the returns brought down the minister states there are several contracts on which a subsequent estimate has been made, and no work done. When he deals with figures in this way, he assumes there will be no extra money paid upon those other contracts. I am dealing with actual results already attained,
I am dealing with figures given to me by the present chief engineer. My hon. friend is making an estimate without information given him by any person on which he could correctly make an estimate.
Does the hon. gentleman pledge his word that the percentage increase on the other eight contracts will be less than upon the thirteen contracts included in the official returns brought down?
I never object to any person asking me a question, but the hon. gentleman knows that that is a question that he should not ask, and that I could not answer.
The reason I ask it is that the minister stated that the alleged error of $16,000,000 is based upon the assumption that there will be no such increase.
I made no such statement, and again I say that the results obtained are based on an estimate made by the chief engineer.

Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask another question -because it is important just now to get 262i
down to hard-pan. There is an increase, according to the returns brought down by the government in thirteen contracts, of 68-8 per cent, and there are eight other contracts. What percentage of increase, if any, has the minister allowed upon thesa other eight contracts in making his statement as to this error?

My hon. friend has asked me another question to which I will reply in the same way that I answered the other one, that the chief engineer, who is a greater authority than any on.e of us upon that point, has given certain "figures, and from these figures I am taking actually what has been paid out and his estimate for the future.

The minister stated a moment ago that he had just seen these figures that required my computation to be amended. Does he forget that on the 31st of March, coming down to the condition we are now dealing with, to the actual figures exclusive of interest, that I presented exactly the same figures then as I presented to-day? And has the minister been able to show that my statement that $104,000,000 was the amount the government showed were expended, of which $60,000,000 in round figures was expended on these thirteen contracts, was incorrect? If he has not, what is he talking about?

My hon. friend is so very polite to-day that I suppose I might answer him in the same way. I am talking about what I think is an error of nearly $16,000,000. I told my hon. friend that I was not surprised that he should make this error in his calculations, and I told the House that I was not finding fault, but in order to be more accurate I was giving my authority for the figures given to me, and if these are correct, he has made a mistake of about $16,000,000.
The minister is aware that he has not answered my question at all.
Because my hon. friend wants me to give an answer to a question which he knows that I, not being an engineer, am not in a position to answer.
It is not an engineering question.
My hon. friend insists on asking me a question which can only be answered on the authority of the chief engineer.
The minister mistakes the question if he says that.

That is my understanding of it. Now, we take up another item-

and I do not want to quarrel with these items-but I want for a moment to take up the Quebec bridge item. Whatever may be said about the Quebec bridge, everybody will admit that the Quebec bridge was a project before there was any thought of the Transcontinental railway. If there had never been a Transcontinental railway built the Quebec bridge would have been constructed. Every person admits that, but I am here to argue that the construction of the Transcontinental railway, instead of being a burden to the people in so far as the Quebec bridge is concerned, is going to assist in bearing that burden. It will assist to the extent of the amount that it will pay either in interest on the cost of construction or in rental for the use of the bridge. The people would have had to build the Quebec bridge had there never been a Transcontinental railway, and this is one more customer to help to pay the interest on the cost of this bridge. Therefore, the Quebec bridge should not be considered as part of the cost of this road. The $7,000,000 that my hon. friend has in his list there should come out because the Quebec bridge should not be part of the Transcontinental railway per se, as the legal gentlemen would say.
Why did the Finance Minister take four-ninths of it into consideration in making up his own estimate in 1903 and 1904?

Because, I presume- and I may say I was not here-that the Transcontinental railway will probably pay an amount equal to four-ninths of the cost of the bridge for the right to run over it. If it is not part of the Transcontinental railway it will pay it in rent. If it is part of the Transcontinental railway it will pay it in interest. Going on a little further mv hon. friend got down to large figures. I have already pointed out a few discrepancies, but I -want to go on a little farther. I do not know what arrangements may be made as to Quebec terminals or the Quebec bridge. These are pretty large questions, and at the present time I could not give an estimate of the cost of the Quebec terminals because the commission has not decided as to what ought to be done there, but they hope to very shortly. I may say for the information of the House that I have suggested that the different railways interested should get together and form some kind of a company or combination by which they would secure the terminals in Quebec as well as the Quebec bridge for their general use. I do not know if that can be carried out, but if it can be carried out to that extent others besides the Transcontinental railway would assist in bearing the burden. It would be a reasonable solution, and it would be the better way of handling the Mr. GRAHAM.
traffic of the city of Quebec. It may not be possible to work it out. but shortly after the House rises I shall endeavour to get the views of the various railways interested in this question, and see what can be accomplished. I find that my hon. friend then makes up an item of $21,000,000 interest. I am not going to stop to quarrel with that, because by making the principal large it is easy enough to make the interest large, but I am going to ask my hon. friend and the House to judge of the fairness of this statement that contains this $42,000,000 the seven years' interest. However, that has nothing to do with what I am going to say now. A few minutes ago my hon. friend-and he says so in the resolution-in figuring out the cost of this railway, made it $218,000,000. He pointed out that at the rate of 3 per cent the fixed charges to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway would be $6,000,000 per year, and he turned around and asked his followers: Will any company pay it? By his own figures he put $42,000,000 into his calculation on which the Grand Trunk will never pay interest and never will be asked to pay under the contract. My hon. friend knows, tins House knows, the country knows that the interest to be paid for seven years does not go into the principal or the rental and is not a fixed charge on the Grand Trunk Pacific. It only shows that my hon. friend has not treated the subject as fairly as he usually does in making out his case. The only result that can be accomplished is to make it difficult for the Grand Trunk Pacific to finance its undertaking, and if that can be accomplished then this road may be crippled, but I want to tell this House that that is not going to be allowed to be done, and that if it were to be the case that the Grand Trunk Pacific did not want this section of the road there is another strong company ready to take it in five minutes and proceed with the running of the road. Now. there can be a difference of opinion about this error of $16,000,000 that I pointed out, but there can be no difference of opinion about the $42,000,000 error, and the hon. gentleman, therefore, knows that this amount does not go into the capital upon which the fixed charge is made. Therefore, is it fair to ask, who is going to run this road?	.

I made the calculation to show what the cost would be at the end of the 3even-year period, and I will challenge the minister, with all his eloquence, with all his extreme energy, to show that the statement is not correct.
My hon. friend will see that he made that statement. I will ask him to deny that he made the statement. Did he not, within the last hour, say that the fixed charges on this road would be $6,000,000?
Yes.
And did not he turn around to his friends and ask: What company will pay it? And did they not say: No?
I quite admit that I mentioned' that the 3um of $6,000,000 would be the fixed charge upon the cost of this railway.
And that some company would have to pay it?

I pointed out that probably the Grand Trunk Pacific would not take over the road, and I was asking if the Grand Trunk Pacific does not take over the road, what position will Canada be in? Is it not a fact that it has a fixed charge, of six and a half million on the actual cost of the construction of the road?

I suppose we must accept this explanation, but I submit again, and I leave it to the hon. gentlemen who responded, when he asked that question: What company would pay this $6,000,000? -to say who is right in this matter. Now, coming to the resolution, we find the same calculation, and I am glad in this instance1 that my hon. friend wrote it down. It says:
Making an average expenditure of more than $120,000 a mile.
That is right.
Does my hon. friend say that when the road is constructed and trains are running on it the road will cost $120,000 a mile?
As far as Canada is concerned, certainly.

The hon. gentleman knows that he made a mistake, and he knows that he cannot get out of it. I have read his resolution. In addition to the $120,000 a mile-and this is the only way in which he can work it out, this is the only way in which he can send the impression to the country-the hon. gentleman proceeds to declare in his resolution:

In the first place the Grand Trunk Pacific Company themselves are contractors, and in so far as they are contractors, section 7 and section 47, would give absolutely no relief, would afford absolutely no safeguard in respect to classification or cost or anything else, because it would be the interest of "the Grand Trunk Pacific to get the highest classification and to make the most they possibly could out of the contract. On the other hand there would be the question so far as they are concerned of the payment of three per cent during a period of 43 years as rental upon that cost. But the country is interested as bearing the ultimate cost and also in the rental which it does not receive during the first seven years. It is interested because it may receive no rental after the expiration of 50 years. It is interested in the rental during the period of 43 years in so far as that rental is less than the interest which this country must pay. I say to my hon. friend the Minister of Raii-ways and Canals, that a parliamentary in-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
vestigation might be necessaary for the very reason that an action had been brought in the Exchequer Court of Canada or an arbitration had taken place under section 47 and that the disclosures in that action, or in that arbitration had shown that parliament ought to take a hand in the proceedings and find out the conditions under which this road had been constructed.
Now, I have disposed of this which was the only argument from the Minister of Railways and Canals which could be dignified by that name. But he went further. He said he was going to show that there was an error of $16,000,000 in the estimate of the hon. member from South Simcoe, and in the terms of this resolution. Did the. Minister of Railways and Canals show an error of $16,000,000. I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals a direct question with regard1 to that. I pointed out to him, or it was pointed out to him in the course of his speech that the hon. member for South Simcoe had made up his statement on a certain basis. What was the basis of the statement of the hon. member for South Simcoe. First that according to the official returns brought down by this government there were 13 contracts which according to the first estimate were to cost $37,340,723. The official return brought down by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals shows that these 13 contracts will cost $60,792,369. My hon. friend for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) took the other 8 contracts. According to the original estimate they were to cost $26,866,054. My hon. friend the member for South Simcoe correctly stated that the 13 contracts had been increased over the original estimate by 62 -8 per cent, and he made a perfectly reasonable, and legitimate argument, that the other eight contracts will be increased in certainly no less a proportion. Therefore we may reasonably exnect that the $26,866,054 will be increased to $43,737,936 or about $16,000,000 more than the original estimate 'made by the government engineer. What was the course of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals? He took that item of $16,000,000, because his argument did not apply to anything else, and he said my hon. friend the member for South Simcoe has made a mistake of $16,000,000. My hon. friend from South Simcoe made no mistake unless he was not justified in applying the same percentage of increase to the eight contracts they had entered upon by the test of experience of the 13 contracts. Yet when I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals across the floor of this House as to whether he was allowing any increase unon these eight contracts I got absolutely no answer, no satisfaction from him in replv to what was a perfectly fair and direct question.

If my hon. friend will allow me, what I said was to try to make it cleaT that my estimate was absolutely made on the estimate and calculation of the chief engineer, and I thought that was the best average I could give. I freely admitted that I did not make the calculation.

That is the way in.
which it was made up. I understood perfectly from the speech of the hon. member for South Simcoe. He took 13 contracts and said the official returns brought down to this House show in respect of these 13 contracts an increase of 62-8 per cent and he said: I take the other 8 contracts, I have the original estimates for the other 8 contracts, and I am perfectly justified in saying that there will be at least as great an increase in respect of these 8 contracts as in respect of the 13 contracts that we know _ about. And the $16,000,000 difference is the alleged mistake pointed out with so much gusto by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals in attempting t-o answer, and a very poor attempt it was, the indictment of my hon. friend from South Simcoe. Well, what becomes then of the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals? Why, Mr. Speaker, it vanishes just as some light sprinkling of snow in May may vanish before the sun as soon as the light is poured in upon it. We say that there is absolutely no foundation whatever, no scintilla of evidence whatever to demonstrate to this House that my hon. friend the member for South Simcoe has made the slightest error in the estimate of the cost of this road.
Well, let us go on. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals and the hon. member from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) ventured upon some verv singular statements in respect of the ' safe-guarding of Canadian ports. I understood both these gentlemen to bewail the fact that the members of the opposition in 1903 and 1904 had not a due, proper and a patriotic regard for the interests of Canadian ports and for the safe-guarding of Canadian traffic through these ports. I do not want to weary this House, but I think this point is of sufficient importance to make it perfectly plain. My hon. friend the member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) has pointed out to this House in his speech this afternoon that the Grand Trunk railway having a great terminal in the United States of America, in the city of Portland, is building a railway and creating another great terminal in the city of Providence, and that the Grand Trunk railway is doing with the express declaration and pledge to the people of Rhode Island and the legislature of Rhode Island, that that city of Providence by means of those terminals and of that railway will be a great port of shipment for the grain
which is to be grown in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, There is absolutely no question about that. If any hon. member of this House ventures to think that these newspaper articles are unfounded, I desire to assure him that I have under my hand here, and can produce, an official stenographic report of the application to the Rhode Island legislature on behalf of the Grand Trunk railway. So, there is^ absolutely no question about the application or about the purpose of the application. Now, how does the government of this country stand in that regard? Are they able to control that situation or are they absolutely unable to control it? And, if they are unable to control that situation, how does it happen that the people of Canada, spending $250,000,000 on this National Transcontinental railway are liable to have the great traffic of the west diverted to ports of the United States? I will tell my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham)-for he was not a member of the government of that time -and does not know anything about these matters-and how it happened. I can tell him that, in 1903, when this measure was being put through the House, a member of the opposition moved this resolution:
That the Grand Trunk Railway of Canada shall covenant and agree as followsThat the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, so long as the Grand. Trunk Company shall control the policy of that company, shall perform, fulfil and carry out, according to the true intent and meaning thereof, all the provisions of the National Transcontinental Railway Act and all the covenants, stipulations and conditions in the schedule agreements, which, according to the terms thereof ought to be performed, fulfilled or carried out by the said Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
And this further resolution was moved by another member of the opposition:
That the Grand Trunk Company shall covenant and agree as follows:-That neither the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company nor the Grand Trunk Company shall in any manner within its power, directly or indirectly, permit, advise or encourage the transportation of traffic by routes or at rates other than those provided in the said agreement and tha't each of the said companies shall in all respects and good faith use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which public aid is granted and accepted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and to Canadian ocean ports.
It is perfectly* true, and I ought to state to the House, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is itself committed to that covenant by the terms of the agreement. What we pointed out, and what I point out now, is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company owns the whole of the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific

Railway Company, and absolutely controls it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) put that in perfectly plain and direct terms and I have his words here under my hand. In 1903, as reported at page 8570 of 'Hansard' of that year, the hon. gentleman said:
We have not been content that they-the Grand Trunk Railway Company-shall stand behind it; we have required and they have readily consented that they shall be in it and of it and form the whole thing.
The Grand Trunk Railway Company is in it, and of it, and forms the whole thing so far as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is concerned. Here was a measure passed upon the recital that its object was to conserve Canadian commerce and traffic to Canadian ports, to protect and safeguard the interests of Canadian ports. And we asked that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, absolutely controlling in everv respect the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, should be bound by the same covenant which was made binding upon the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, receiving through the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company enormous aid for the construction of this transcontinental railway, should not be at liberty to divert traffic brought over the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to its terminals in Portland or elsewhere in the United States. And my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals sits upon the same treasury benches with the gentleman who absolutely refused to accept that amendment, and absolutely refused to impose any stipulation whatever upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company in that regard. So that, to-day we have a singular position. I have not heard that the Grand Trunk Railway Company or the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are purchasing any lands or building any terminals in the city of Halifax. The Minister of Railways and Canals has told us twice in this House during the present session that he has heard that they are buying some lands in the city of St. John. Up to the present time that is only a rumour. But it is not a rumour so far as Providence, R.I., is concerned. They have gone before the legislature of that state and they propose to expend $10,000,000 or $15,000,000 in developing an American port. _ And they propose that this railway, which according to the ex-deputy Minister Railways and Canals, as reported in the public press, will cost $350,000,000-

Well, the position is that this Toad, costing the people of this country at least $250,000,000, is to he used for the purpose of building up and developing a great port in the United States of America. What about the recital of the agreement? What about the stipulation that we asked to have made binding on the Grand Trunk Railway Company? What have the gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches to say in regard to that object? I understand that the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company has said that Providence, Rhode Island, is to be used as an overflow. There is nothing in the address of his counsel which indicates that; there is nothing in the reports which appeared in the Providence newspapers to indicate that. Is there any reason why Providence, Rhode Island, should be equipped at enormous cost for the purpose of carrying and receiving traffic from our Northwest, while not a finger is being lifted or a dollar spent to develop St. John and Halifax in that regard? The situation is a most remarkably peculiar one, Mr. Speaker, and one which, I think, demands the attention of this government. Let us 'ook at the circumstances for a moment. I have the figures, but I will content myself with speaking in general terms. The Grand Trunk Railway Company can haul grain to Portland at less cost than it can haul it to St. John or Halifax, for the distance is shorter. It is bound under the contract to make the rates to St. John and Halifax the same as to Portland; it is bound-if I understand the terms of the contract correctly-to make the rates to St. John and Halifax, the same as to Providence.
Well then if it gets the same rate for St. John and Halifax that it gets for Providence and Portland, and if ^ in hauling grain to St. John and Halifax it is obliged to give a certain proportion of the haulage to the Intercolonial, will its interests lie in the direction of St. John and Halifax, or will they lie in the direction of Portland and Providence? Is there any question about that? The members of the government, when we put that point up to them, over and over again in debate were obliged to admit what I am saying now. Then does not every circumstance emphasize the absolute necessity that existed when this contract went through the House, that there should have been some stipulation inserted binding the Grand Trunk Company to conserve the interest of our Canadian ports? My hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Magrath) to-day said something with which I absolutely concur; he said the Grand Trunk Company having its interests to carry to" Portland and Providence, would do so, and that in doing so it would only

exercise good business sense. I entirely concur in that view from their standpoint. I find no fault with the Grand Trunk Railway Company for making the best bargain they could, but I denounce this government for having been weak enough absolutely to refuse the imposition of any stipulation or safeguard whatever which would prevent the Grand Trunk Company from doing that very thing. The financial aid contributed by the maritime provinces towards the construction of this railway will not fall short of $35,000,000 or $40,000,000, and if the poTts of Halifax and St. John are to have no safeguard whatever that that enormous grain trade of the west will go in the winter months at least to the ports of Halifax and St. John, I ask whether a contract such as this is to be regarded as fair, just and reasonable to the interests of the maritime provinces. I unhesitatingly declare that it cannot be so regarded. And so, Mr. Speaker, the circumstances to-day suggest either that the government is either in a position to deal with this proposed diversion of traffic to the terminals of the Grand Trunk Railway at Portland and Providence, or it is not; if it is not capable of dealing with the situation, then its incapacity is due to its own default, to its refusal in 1903 and 1904 to impose any stipulation or condition upon the Grand Trunk Railway in that respect. I say if the government are in a position to deal with this question, they should take the matter into immediate consideration and act at once in such a manner as to conserve the interests of the maritime ports of Canada; if they are in a position to do that, if they are absolutely incapable under the terms of the contract they have made of conserving and preserving the interests of the maritime ports, then I say that,	in	all fairness
and in all honour, they ought to give up the seals of office, resign their seats, and give place to men who are actuated by a more patriotic regard for the true interests of this country.
