Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, although the hour is iate, I take this opportunity of adverting again to a matter which was brought to the attention of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) on April 14. That is the release in a summary manner of the two men, King and Skill, who, upon their own admission, were found guilty of selling and distributing obscene literature. The matter was first brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice on the 14th April, and not then being in a position to give any definite information to the House he postponed his answer until the following day, when he gave to the House certain reasons why he had recommended executive clemency to these men. The reasons given by the hon. gentleman on that day are somewhat extraordinary. I do not desire, Sir, to comment upon any reasons which may have guided the Minister of Justice in recommending executive clemencv where he thought the circumstances of the case were such as to call for the exercise of the prerogative of the Crown. But when an hon. gentleman presents a statement such as that put forward in this case I think it calls for some comment, as it has called for considerable comment of a public nature from sources which are generally in sym- ' pathy with whatever views the hon. gentleman advances in this House. But before I refer to that, I would like to remind the hon. gentleman of the concluding paragraph of the speech in which he gave his reasons for recommending executive clemency in this case.

I seek to put no responsibility upon him in this matter.
That is referring to the Attorney General of Ontario.
I willingly assume the whole responsibility myself, I gave the advice to His Excellency that these men should be summarily released, because, in my humble judgment, speaking as a lawyer, they were rot guilty of the offence with which they were charged.
It was not, therefore, a recommendation of executive clemency. It was a statement of the Governor General that these men had been improperly convicted. These men were represented by three eminent counsel in Toronto, and upon the recommendation and advice of these counsel who had seen the literature they pleaded guilty of the offence with which they were charged, and they were severely reprimanded by the learned judge, and were sentenced to one year's imprisonment in the central prison. The Minister of Justice recommends their summary release, because in his opinion as a lawyer they were not guilty of the offences with which they were charged. I do not want to add any more comment: I think the paper I have in my hand is sufficient comment to pass upon the matter, and I think possibly it may appeal to the Prime Minister, coming from the source it does. I refer to the Toronto 'Globe' of April 21, 1910, a leading article which reads as if it came from the pen of the reverend editor himself. It is as follows :
April 21, 1910.
The abuse of executive clemency.
The time has come for great plainness of speech. In the name of everything decent and clean in Canadian life the 'Globe' makes deliberate and emphatic public protest against tile clemency of the Crown being extended to men convicted of traffic in obscene pictures and vilely immoral books. This public protest is made necessary by a suspicious laxness in prosecuting such offenders shown from time to_ time by subordinate Crown officials, and still more by the occasional pardon or release from prison of vicious-minded convicts whose trade in life was more pernicious than a pestilence. Words need not be minced. The 'Globe' protests, for instance, against the release of King and Skill. These two traffickers in prurient and licentious books were sentenced, on their own plea of guilty, to one year in the Central Prison, and their release after serving two months was defended in parliament by the Minister of Justice on Friday last. The 'Globe' protests even more emphatically against the defence offered for their release. This case and other instances in subordinate courts make the situation utterly intolerable.
In parliament the Minister of Justice defended his action in recommending the clemency of the Crown. He represented that the books are 'classics.' He admitted that they contain 'passages' which if singled out or collected and published together might properly be described by the word 'indecent;' but in
this respect he said they were not different from 'that best of books we all revere.' The minister stated that he had 'letters with regard to this case urging clemency' from 'a bishop of the Protestant faith, three other clergymen, one a leading clergyman in the Methodist Church,' 'who are acquainted with the prisoners and knew the style of business that they had been carrying on.' The Minister of Justice made reference to 'a personal discussion of the case with the Attorney General of the province of Ontario,' who 'in his capacity of Attorney General of the province wrote a candid, frank letter expressing his own views and his own recommendation in regard to the case.' The minister closed his speech as reported in 'Hansard' with these words: 'I gave the advice to His Excellency that these men should be summarily re leased, because, in my humble judgment, speaking as a lawyer, they were not guilty of the offence with which they were charged.'
In the clear light of known facts all this conduct on the part of the Ministers of the Crown and of the ministers of the church is inexplicable where it is not impious. It is not a fact, as the Minister of Justice states, that 'the learned judge, upon the admitted facts of the case, made a conviction.' Judge Winchester did not need to make a conviction. The two men pleaded guilty. They did so on advice of eminent counsel, and that, too, after many weeks of delay and the exercise of all the arts and ingenuities by which the giving of evidence in open court is avoided. The evidence of the Crown was damning to the last degree and its publication would have shocked the public. The chief coroner of Toronto, to whom the books were referred for report by the Crown, testified that they are absolutely without scientific value, and 'are unutterably vile, reeking with filth from beginning to end. After a careful examination of a dozen of these books, the 'Globe' endorses that judgment of Dr. Arthur Jukes Johnson. Their only value to science is as samples of the erotic factors in the making of degenerates and perverts. As literature they range all the way from the scrofulous French novel, uuexpurged, vilely illustrated, and elegantly hound, to the still more lecherous exposition and advocacy of the grossest unnatural sensuality.
How comes it, then, that the persistent and even defiant purveyors of this corrupt, and corrupting literature, having pleaded their guilt in open court, were 'summarily released' on the advice of the Minister of Justice? How comes it that, as he declared in parliament. sucli executive clemency was 'urged' by ' a Protestant bishop and a leading clergyman in the Methodist Church' and ' recommended' by the Attorney General of Ontario? The only answer the 'Globe' can give is that no one of these gentlemen-not the minister, not the Attorney General, not the bishop, not the clergyman-could have had personal knowledge of the essential facts. Their ignorance is their excuse. But in this case and under its circumstances to give 'character' letters or to recommend clemency without knowing the facts was itself inexcusable, while to do it with a knowledge of the facts wTould have been criminal.	_
But the obscene picture postcard is even more of a leprous plague than the immoral book. Many of those books are expensive,

while the cards are scattered broadcast in every part of Canada, polluting boys and girls in the schools, and leaving on their minds and memories scars which neither repentance nor lifelong experience will wholly; eradicate. Last week the police authorities in Toronto destroyed 87,000 picture cards of unimaginable obscenity, taken from a man now serving sentence, but for whom, the 'Globe' is informed, the clemency of the Crown is now being urged. More than 50,000 of such cards were circulated in Toronto a few months ago, and thousands of others were sold to towns in Ontario. They are all unspeakably vile. And yet for the assassins of youthful purity who engage in this business, the protection of the Crown is claimed. Such a thing would violate every sense of decency and would rightly involve all parties to it in shame and inevitable disgrace.
The 'Globe' offers no apology for this protest. It will not cease its open denunciation so long as the need remains. This is a matter neither of politics nor of law, but of fundamental morality, and touches the very life of the nation. No quarter can be given in Canada to the vices that ruined ancient Rome and are sapping the virility of modern Europe. Of those corroding vices, the immoral book and the obscene picture are the chief agents. Every citizen, who is not a traitor to private decency and national character, must stand unflinchingly against what makes only for decay.
Those are not my comments on the matter, they are the comments of the Toronto ' Globe,' after, as I understand it, a personal inspection of the literature which formed the subject of the charge. Unless I am incorrectly informed the Prime Minister has been interviewed in regard to this subject. He has been shown some of this literature and is in a position to make a public statement as to whether he agrees with the Minister of Justice in the view he takes, both with regard to law and fact in recommending what he is pleased to call executive clemency in this case. I think it only fair to draw public attention to this article in the ' Globe,' the chief organ of the government in Ontario, in order that both the right hon. the Prime Minister and the hon. the Minister of Justice may have an opportunity to publicly state in this House, what their views are with respect to offences of this kind.
I have read in another papeT, a letter from a gentleman holding a high position in one of the churches of Ontario, in which he makes a comment, which is very unfair, that a gentleman holding a seat in the House of Commons, not behind the government, he is careful to say, is seeking to obtain some public notoriety by bringing this matter to the attention of the House. There is only one hon. member to whom that letter can refer and that is myself. I resent it utterly. I made no comment on the case, I did not even ask the Minister of Justice if the article in the ' Canadian Municipal Journal,' to which I drew his attention as Minister of Justice on April Mr. BOYCE.
14, was true or not, but I felt it was proper to bring an item like that .to the attention of the government and especially of the minister, in order that such explanation might be given as was called for by the nature of the article which imputed directly to the Minister of Justice, that these men were released as a result of the exercise of political pressure upon him. speechtext: It will lie in your memory, Mr. Speaker, and in the memory I have no doubt of every member of this House, that when this matter was first brought to the attention of the House by the hon. gentleman, it was by the reading of an ar.ticle in some Montreal newspaper, in which the charge was made, not in any insinuating or disguised form, but in so many words, that these particular prisoners, who had been pardoned then some six weeks or two months before, had been released solely and only because the application for their pardon was made by Mr. Robinette of Toronto, who was said to be a personal friend of my own, and a man who had a pull with me in matters of this kind. That was the gravamen of the charge which the hon. gentleman made, or w'hich he endorsed to the exent of reading the article in question and asking some statement from me on the subject.
Mr. Speaker, I must ask permission to correct the hon. gentleman in that statement. I neither made nor endorsed any charge at all in reference to this, matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have read what the hon. gentleman said when he brought the article to which I have referred to the attention of the House. In saving that he endorsed the article to the extent he did, I mean that he took the responsibility that I suppose any hon. member of this House takes when he reads in the House an article from a newspaper, and asks or suggests that there should be some explanation in regard to it, made by the membei of the House against whom it is levelled I need not stop to discuss whether that con stitutes an endorsation of the charge or not The question I want to bring to the atten tion of the House is whether the recommen dation I made to His Excellency in this

matter was an honest and bona fide exercise of the responsibility which is placed upon me in that regard, or was something which I had done improperly, and as I would think dishonourably, and in contravention of the duty which is put upon me-if I had in fact acted as the newspaper which was read in so many words charged. With regard to this whole matter, I have nothing to say in addition to what I have already said in this House, unless it may be to say that if the same thing were to be considered over again, under the same circumstances, I should act in exactly the way in which I have acted throughout. I have taken the course which I thought was right, and which I still think was right, I am sorry if my hon. friend cannot concur in it. I am very sorry if the learned gentleman to whom he refers as in his opinion the writer of some editorial comments upon my action which appeared in the ' Globe,' newspaper does not concur in the course I took. I have nothing to say in that regard except that the writer of that article is as entitled to his opinion as everybody else in this country is entitled to his opinion in the matter. But the important thing to be borne in mind is that this prerogative of pardon, one of the most important, possibly the most important, of the remaining prerogatives of the Crown, is one which under our system of government cannot be exercised upon the personal responsibility of His Majesty or Mis Majesty's representative in this country. The action which was taken in this matter, and which is taken in any of these cases, is something which can properly be taken only upon the advice of some person who is responsible for that ae tion. I do not know that I can take any exception to the phrase which the hon. gentleman has used to-night, that these men-were summarily released by me. Of course, that is not strictly accurate, as every one knows. My action in the matter was not to order any release; it was to recommend, and I take the whole responsibility for what was done. I thought I made that as clear as I could in what I said on this subject some days ago. I have never sought to place any responsibility upon the legal gentlemen who applied for the release of their -clients, who urged that release^ who made their representations,_ and their pleas for clemency or for executive action in the way of the granting of a pardon. No more did I seek or do I seek to put any responsibility in the matter on the men in the various walks of life, to whom I alluded in speaking be fore, who did not sign petitions, but who wrote independent letters to me on the subject, each urging in his own way his own view. Nor did I ever seek to put the slightest responsibility in the matter upon the learned Attorney General for the province
of Ontario. That gentleman has, according to this morning's Toronto newspapers, made a statement with regard to the letter which he wrote to me in connection with this matter, a statement which I need not say is entirely in accordance with the facts, which gives the purport of his letter, as it was his privilege to do if he saw fit, though I certainly would not have considered that I had any right to give to the public the contents or the substance of a letter which he had written to me on such a subject. I put no responsibility whafi ever upon him in the matter. I do not seek to say that his advice or his views influenced me in the matter. I take the whole responsibility for what was done, be cause it was upon my advice, and my advice alone that His Excellency was pleased to exercise his power of pardon in the premises. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the House that_this responsibility is not a responsibility upon any of my colleagues-is not a responsibility upon the government as a whole. The instructions to His Excellency from His Majesty himself, under his own hand, are that in the exercise of the prerogative of pardon he is to be guided by the advice of his minister, not by the advice of his Council; and His Excellency acted in this matter upon my sole advice, without my having conferred with any of my colleagues, without there being the slightest responsibility upon the First Minister, or upon any other member of the cabinet. Now,, the question is, was I wrong? If I was wrong, I trust that the hon. gentleman, and every other hon. member of this House, will acquit me of the original charge, the charge that was made in connection with this case, as I am sorry to say it has been made with reference to the same Mr. Robinette on other occasions by other members of this House, that because of the man who applied, and because it was Mr. Robinette, some course was taken in the matter which otherwise would not have been taken. That charge, at any rate, hon. gentlemen see for themselves, has not a particle of foundation.
If I made a mistake it was an error of judgment. I have the satisfaction of knowing that it received the approval of His Excellency and I cannot refrain from saying that I value, in a matter of this kind at all events, the approval of His Excellency the present Governor General of this country far and away beyond any importance I would attach to the approval of the editor of the Toronto ' Globe.' I based my action in this matter as I stated to the House the other day simply and entirely upon the fact that as a lawyer I was of opinion that those men by selling the books in question, which it was admitted . they had done, had not committed the of-

fence with which they were charged. I say nothing as to whether they had committed some other offence. The question did not arise for consideration. They were charged with distributing literature which was obscene in character. I mentioned, when speaking before, some of the authors whose works were in question. I referred to those authors whom I mentioned as classics. I have nothing to modify in that respect. I did not pretend to say that those writers whose names I mentioned were the only writers. I stated on the contrary, that there were others, that there were some of the more modern French school. I did not refer to those modern writers as classics. I do not know whether the term could or could not properly be applied to them. The question which was presented for consideration here was upon the undisputed facts of the case, whether or not the books which were in evidence, which were marked by the officer of the court and sent by him to me, were books which properly fell within the meaning of the word ' obscene ' .as used in the particular section of the Criminal Code upon which this charge was founded. I do not know whether all the members of this House would understand the same thing as the meaning of the word ' obscene ' that I understand bv it. I have simply to say that having examined those books which were sent to me bv the officer of the court as being the books in question they did not constitute such literature as I understand would be, as a matter of law, covered by the term ' obscene That is the whole question of the conclusion to which I came in this matter. I looked upon it as entirely a lawyer's question. Long explanations were given of the reason which had led the legal advisers of the prisoners, advising them to enter a plea of guilty. Statements as to why that was done, how it came to be done are matters which I need not enter into, and which I may say at once did not influence me. I do not think that in a case which has been disposed of by a court we need enter into a consideration of what the reasons were which led learned counsel for the defendants to take a particular course in court, and certainly I am not passing one way or the other upon any question of the wisdom of the course which was so advised. The1;, whole importance of the matter is this, that there was no dispute about the facts of the case. The books were there. They had been sold by those particular prisoners. That was admitted, and the question was simply whether the sale of those particular books did or did not, as a matter of law, constitute an offence within that particular section of the Code. I have merely to repeat that in my humble opinion as a lawyer, it did not constitute any such offence. Having reached that clear conclu-aion about which I felt no hesitation at Mr. AYLESWORTH.
the time, about which I certainly feel no hesitation now, and in respect to which I am not in the least degree influenced by anything which has appeared in the newspapers, I adhere to the opinion upon which I acted in advising His Excellency that the thing which those two men confessedly had done did not constitute the particular offence which was described by that section of the Act. I regard that as a pure question of dry law and though I may have my opinion other lawyers may have an opposite opinion, or men who are not lawyers such as the writer in the ' Globe ' i-, I presume, may have a different opinion. As to that, I have nothing in the world to say. Many a time before now I have found gentlemen more learned in the law than I am, having a different opinion from mi no on matters of law.. I have never resented it or considered I had any grievance because they expressed it. In this particular matter I may have a feeling that an attempt has been made to divert popular attention from the real truth of the matter, and from the real facts of the case as I put them before the House when speaking previously. I have simply to rest upon the statement which I made before, ar.d which I am repeating now, that this was a question entirely of law as I understood it then, and as I understand it now, and if 1 have made a mistake in this matter it is just like a great many other mistakes that I have made in matters of law in my time in coming to a conclusion upon a legal question which was in truth erroneous though I honestly believed it to he correct.

Ottawa, April 11, 1910. Hon. Geo. P. Graham, P.C.,
Minister of Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
Sir,-In compliance with your verbal request, I have the honour to submit herewith, on behalf of the commissioners, a statement furnishing the information requested by Mr. R. L. Borden, M.P., leader of the opposition, as reported on page 5385 of f Hansard ' (unrevised edition); also a statement from our

chief engineer setting forth the data upon which were based the estimates of the quantities made by the engineers before the work was opened up and the several contracts let, which includes an explanation for the apparent discrepancy between the quantities as originally estimated and as returned under the various contracts.
To make clear the distinction between ' solid rock ' as generally understood by the layman, and ' solid rock ' within the meaning of the general specifications for construction, it may as well, at the outset, to quote the approved interpretation of clause 34 of the specifications defining solid rock excavation, as made by the chief engineer, in January, 1908.
Clause 34-solid rock excavation-reads as follows:-
Solid rock excavation will include all rock found in ledges or masses of more than one cubic yard, which, in the judgment of the engineer, may be best removed by blasting.
The chief engineer's approved interpretation of the above is as follows:-
I am of the opinion that rock found in ledges or masses as specified must (firstly) be rock, and (secondly) it must be in ledges, conglomerate form (known as plum pudding stone), boulders, or ledge rock displaced (in pieces each exceeding one cubic yard in size), rock assembled, also shale rock, such as in the judgment of the engineer may be best removed by blasting.
Accompanying the foregoing interpretation is a diagram in explanation.
When the discrepancies in quantities of solid rock, loose rock, and common excavation as between those estimated by the engineers before the ground was broken and the contracts let, and those actually returned under the several contracts first became manifest; and when difficulties in matters of classification, &c., became apparent in Major Hoclgins' district east of Winnipeg, realizing that, however inaccurate the original estimates might have been, the real and predominating question affecting the public interest was to see that what was returned and paid for _ as solid rock was actually solid rock within the meaning of the specifications; and that, similarly, what was returned and paid for as loose rock was properly classifiable as such under the general specifications for construction; the commissioners determined on the appointment of an inspecting engineer whose duty it would he, under the direction _ and subject to the instructions of the chief engineer, to go over the line, and report directly to the chief engineer on _ all matters of classification, &c., along the line under construction. Accordingly. on Mr. Lumsden's recommendation, Mr. Gordon Grant, the present chief engineer of the commission, was, on the 16th of May, 1907, appointed inspecting engineer.
There appears to be a disposition in some quarters to give currency to the view that where, say 1,000 cubic yards of solid rock *Were originally estimated by the engineers before the work was opened up, and 1,250 or 1,500 cubic yards have been actually returned by the engineers under the contracts, that the difference represents and must be overclassification, or the improper transfer of 250 or 500 cubic yards, as the case may be, from the loose rock or common excavation column into the solid rock column, and that the contractor is paid at the higher rate when he should be paid at the lower. Of course nothing could be more misleading.
Any layman can understand how difficult it is for an engineer to go over a piece of country, particularly if it be a timbered country, with heavy side hills, &c., and estimate exactly, or even very approximately, tlie number of cubic yards of solid rock (even if that be confined to ledge rock and boulders over a cubic yard iu size) in hills, &c., down to a certain grade line.
In the case of contracts Nos. 9 and 10 (150 miles from the Quebec bridge westerly), the quantities were estimated partly on a first location, partly on preliminary, and partly on projected lines and after the crn-tracts had been awarded, it was found necessary to change the location of the line in several places, thus vitiating the value of the original estimates of quantities as a basis of comparison, while at the same time improving the line; in district ' F,' in the case of contract No. 21 (McArthur contract), no allowance was made in the engineers' estimates of quantities for excavation of one foot below grade in rock cuttings; nor was any allowance made for the removal of material outside the regular slopes in rock cuttings or rock borrow; all borrow for fills was estimated as common excavation, although after the work was opened up it was found that from the Canadian Pacific railway crossing at Rennie to Superior Junction, a distance of about 180 miles, the country is all rock; and in district ' A,' from Moncton to the Quebec boundary, there was no outcropping of reck shown on or near the line.
These are some of the reasons accounting for the apparent discrepancy between the quantities as estimated before the ground was broken and the contracts awarded, and as returned under the various contracts. It will be doubtless contended that much more accurate estimates might have obtained had tlie engineers been required to make borings say every one hundred yards over the entire 1,804 miles of line between Winnipeg and Moncton. And this is readily admitted. But, to have done so would have required a large additional expenditure of time and money before the actual work of construction was commenced on any single contract, without any saving in the co-t of construction; such a course, our engineers advise, is rarely, if ever, followed in this country, as it is not believed that the results warrant the additional expenditure of time and money involved.
As has already been pointed out, the important thing is to see that the contractors shall be paid for only what they are entitled to under the general specifications governing the construction of the railway, and that the work is executed up to the standard required. The commissioners believe that they have taken every possible precaution to safeguard the public interest along these lines. Two inspecting engineers reporting directly to the chief engineer are practically continuously going over the work in the different districts. In addition, there are the inspecting engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Com-

pany constantly passing on tlie work as it is performed, and when they do not agree with the engineers of the commission as to the work, their complaints are promptly filed in writing, to be passed upon by a board of experts acting as arbitrators under the authority of the National Transcontinental Railway Act. It would be difficult indeed to suggest any safeguards to protect the public interests which do not already exist on this work.
With respect to the cost of the line, the fact cannot be too much emphasized or too frequently repeated, that when the National Transcontinental Railway is completed, the people of Canada will have a railway constructed to a standard of perfection with respect to gradients and curvature, character of roadbed, and permanency of structures (such as steel bridges and viaducts, culverts, &c.,) which but few railways in the world can equal. Railways such as the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk have within the past ten or fifteen years expended many millions of dollars to bring their lines in some places up to the standard which will prevail over the entire National Transcontinental Railway. The costs of operation wrill be infinitesimal in comparison with those of lines having ruling gradients of one per cent, and the benefits of this economy in operation should accrue to the people of Canada, not only through the development of the country through which the railway runs, but also, eventually, in materially reduced freight and passenger rates.

The equipment bonds are not a lien upon the equipment?
No, I think not, in the sense the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. Haggart) means.

I do not like to ask too many questions to-night; the minister seemed to think this afternoon that he had given me to-o much information. I hope he will not think there is any hard feeling between us if I ask a question or two. What is the position of the arbitration proceedings of the three engineers under, as the minister alleges, clause 7 of the agreement? Have they gone to work this spring?

I have been making inquiries for the last few -days as to what day they would resume, as they had started. I understand that they hope that the conditions along the line will soon enable them to do work.
Nothing this spring?
No.

I think the minister is mistaken in saying that they did anything as an arbitration. I saw, by a return moved for by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) that the members of the arbitration had met at

Winnipeg and proceeded on the line, but found it was too late in the year. The snow was on, and they could not make inspection. Then, the engineer of the company and Mr. Gordon Grant went together and made some adjustments. I think that that is as much as has been done.

The three arbitrators went out on the question of overbreak. As a matter of fact, the weather would not permit measurements in regard to classification. But the chief engineer of the Transcontinental and the chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific agreed to about 70 per cent of the differences between them on overbreak.
No arbitrator?

There will .be no arbitration except as to the thirty per cent remaining, but on this the arbitrators will have to act.
